name: Giant Dipper (Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk)

name: Casino and Cocoanut Grove (Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk)

Weeks; Name: the ballroom became the Cocoanut Grove during Prohibition; Model: outline from OpenStreetMap (© OSM contributors, ODbL) (52.7 × 66.8 m); roof levels measured on the 2020 USGS lidar: block 13 m, ballroom roof 17 m, the rounded beach pavilion 17–19 m (its high roof 14 m across); pavilion drum (radius 10 m) fitted to the OSM outline; colonnade, roof forms and colours estimated; the 1907 building had Moorish domes and has been altered — drawn in its present massing for every year (earlier roofline LOW CONFIDENCE)

name: The Plunge natatorium / Neptune's Kingdom (Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk)

name: Looff Carousel (Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk)
notes: Construction 1911.2–1911.6; Built: 1911: carousel bought new from Charles I. D. Looff's factory in Long Beach, with 73 carved horses; its 342-pipe band organ was built in 1894; National Historic Landmark with the Giant Dipper (1987); Model: round building outline from OpenStreetMap (© OSM contributors, ODbL) (21.5 m across); eave 4 m, conical roof to 10 m and cupola to 12.3 m measured on the 2020 USGS lidar; colours estimated

name: Santa Cruz Municipal Wharf
notes: Construction 1913.6–1914.93; 2024: about 150 ft at the end collapsed in high surf on Dec 23, 2024 (drawn at full length); Built: opened Dec 5, 1914 — the most recent of six wharves built on this site; base of the north Monterey Bay fishing fleet; Size: 2,745 ft (837 m) long before the 2024 storm — the longest pier on the West Coast; Model: deck outline and the buildings on it from OpenStreetMap (© OSM contributors, ODbL; buildings as rectangles); deck level 7.0 m (NAVD88) and building heights from the 2020 USGS lidar; pile count and spacing schematic; roofs simplified

name: Mission Santa Cruz (adobe church)
notes: Construction 1793.15–1794.36; Built: mission founded Aug 28, 1791 on the river flat and moved up to the hill by 1793; the first permanent church, of adobe with a stone front, was completed and dedicated in 1794; Size: 112 ft long, 29 ft wide, 25 ft high, walls 5 ft thick, with a stone front; Fate: the bell tower fell in the 1840 earthquake; the front wall and much of the church collapsed after the Fort Tejon earthquake of Jan 9, 1857; the ruin was cleared for Holy Cross Church (1889); Model: documented length, width and wall height; placed on the axis of Holy Cross Church, which was built "over (in the same orientation) part of the original sanctuary and cemetery" — exact position, roof pitch, front and door estimated; the bell tower (no dimensions) is not modelled (LOW CONFIDENCE)

name: Holy Cross Church (Santa Cruz)
notes: Construction 1888–1889.7; Built: 1889: Gothic Revival brick parish church built over part of the mission church's sanctuary and cemetery, in the same orientation (a wooden church of 1858 had stood next door); Height: spire 45.0 m (148 ft), nave ridge 21.5 m, eaves 12.9 m — measured on the 2020 USGS lidar; Model: nave 19 × 28 m, raised sanctuary roof (24 m), apse and the tower (7.6 m square below, 5.9 m above 22 m, a 3.7 m octagonal stage from 28 to 37 m under the spire) placed from the lidar (the OpenStreetMap outline, used for the footprint it replaces, lies ≈ 6 m further south); pinnacles, door and colours estimated; construction start estimated

name: Mission Santa Cruz (1931 replica chapel)

name: Santa Cruz Lighthouse (1869)
notes: Construction 1869.5–1869.95; Built: wooden lighthouse on a brick foundation, built in the summer of 1869 from the plans of the Ediz Hook light (Washington Territory): a one-and-a-half-storey keeper's house with a pitched roof and a square light tower; fifth-order Fresnel lens first lit Jan 1, 1870; Moved: in 1879, with sea caves cutting under the point, it was jacked up and rolled about 300 ft north (drawn at that second site throughout); Fate: replaced in Feb 1941 by a 26 ft wooden framework tower 200 ft seaward; sold in 1948 and dismantled for its lumber from May 20, 1948; Model: no dimensions found: house (8.6 × 10.4 m) and tower (≈ 11.4 m to the lantern roof) estimated from photographs; placed about 300 ft north of the tip of Lighthouse Point, ± 40 m (LOW CONFIDENCE)

name: Mark Abbott Memorial Lighthouse
notes: Construction 1967–1967.9; Built: 1967: brick lighthouse given by the parents of Mark Abbott, who drowned bodysurfing off Pleasure Point on Feb 28, 1965; it took over from the Coast Guard's 1941 framework tower. Since June 1986 it houses the Santa Cruz Surfing Museum; Tower: 39 ft (12 m) square brick tower attached to a one-storey brick building; focal plane 60 ft; Model: footprint from OpenStreetMap (© OSM contributors, ODbL; 6.8 × 11.2 m); tower position (north-west end), its 3.9 m square and 11.9 m top checked on the 2020 USGS lidar (building 7.1 m wide); lantern proportions estimated

name: Walton Lighthouse (Santa Cruz Breakwater Light)
notes: Construction 2001.3–2001.95; Built: 2001: the current light on the west jetty of the Santa Cruz Small Craft Harbor (first breakwater light 1964); named for Charles Walton, who gave much of its cost in memory of his brother Derek, a merchant seaman; Tower: 41.5 ft (12.6 m) tapered cylindrical tower with balcony and lantern, white with a narrow green band; focal plane 59.5 ft; Model: position and height (12.8 m above the jetty) from the 2020 USGS lidar, 3 m south of the OpenStreetMap node; taper and lantern proportions estimated

name: SS Palo Alto, the "Cement Ship" (Seacliff)
notes: Construction 1930.06–1930.49; Built: concrete tanker launched at Oakland on May 29, 1919, too late for the war and never in service; sold as a hulk in 1924; Seacliff: bought by the Seacliff Amusement Corporation, towed from Oakland on Jan 21–22, 1930 and sunk on the sea floor off the beach on Jan 25, bow to the waves; with a dance floor, a café and a swimming pool it opened on June 28, 1930; the company failed in 1932, the ship was stripped, bought by the State for $1 in 1936 and used as a fishing pier; Size: 420 ft between perpendiculars, 434 ft (132 m) overall, beam 54 ft, depth 35 ft; Fate: a crack of 1932 split the hull in a 1963 storm; closed 1980–83 and again from 2016; a storm tore the stern off on Jan 21, 2017; drawn whole; Model: hull outline from OpenStreetMap (© OSM contributors, ODbL; 130.4 × 17.5 m, bow seaward); deck ≈ 5.6 m and the ends ≈ 8 m above sea level after what is left on the 2020 USGS lidar (3–9 m); the 1930 dance hall, café and pool are not modelled

name: Seacliff pier (to the Cement Ship)
notes: Construction 1930–1930.45; Built: 1930: timber pier from the beach to the grounded SS Palo Alto — 630 ft long and 40 ft wide, finished in early June 1930 (other accounts say 500 or 600 ft); Fate: a fishing pier of Seacliff State Beach from 1936; wrecked by storm surf on Jan 5, 2023 and removed; Model: measured on the 2020 USGS lidar: deck 6.45 m (NAVD88), 12.2 m (40 ft) wide, 190 m (623 ft) from the ship to the beach; piles schematic

name: Capitola Wharf
notes: Construction 1856.8–1857.5; Built: 1857: a 450 ft wharf, "Soquel Landing", built for F. A. Hihn by the carpenter Sedgwick Lynch; lengthened to 1,200 ft within a few years; today 855 ft (261 m); Storms: surf broke the wharf in two in January 2023; rebuilt with new piles and a deck widened from 20 to 36 ft, reopened Sep 25, 2024; Model: today's outline for every year since 1857 (OpenStreetMap, © OSM contributors, ODbL — the 20 ft deck before the 2024 widening; 264 m long); deck level 7.0 m (NAVD88) from the 2020 USGS lidar; the 19th-century wharf differed in length (LOW CONFIDENCE before the 20th century); the buildings at its head (bait shop, restaurant; removed 2024) are not modelled; piles schematic

name: Felton Covered Bridge
